speechtext:

subsubtopic: STUDY TEAM'S REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the study team report on Indian and native programs shows at best a limp grasp and, at worst, a profound misunderstanding of the aspirations, needs, and living situations of Canada's First Nations citizens.
The good ideas in it are, almost without exception, repetitions of issues raised by First Nations' organizations, the
Auditor General, and even the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. The misconceptions are profound, even appalling. For example, they state at page 13 that 70 per cent of status Indians will be incarcerated by age 25, and, at page 23, that existing Government programs are "recreating modern suburbs in the northern bush". My riding includes one in every eleven Indian bands in Canada and there is perhaps one community that even faintly resembles that ludicrous description.
On page 69 we find the statement: "There would probably be better results if more of the investments were for the purpose of taking over established successful operations". I wish the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) had considered that before he sabotaged the Native Economic Development Program application of the Yukon Indian Development Corporation.

subsubtopic: EXAMINATION OF OPTIONS ADVOCATED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the report of the Task force on Program Review has opened the door to an opportunity for Canadians. This report and its options should be carefully examined.
In national policy-making, an unswerving adherence to the status quo is often a self-defeating exercise which prevents growth, development, and progress. I encourage all Canadians to participate in a constructive national questioning of the status quo.
Thoughtful people should agree that it is healthy for a nation to assess, challenge, and test its long-held approaches and policies. It would be regrettable if some political Parties would prefer grandstanding instead of a positive national dialogue. Here exists an opportunity for all of us, opposing as our viewpoints might be, to discuss options in a conciliatory and rational debate and then decide which proposals we should accept and which we should reject.

The Bill would apply all the criteria presently stipulated for a Firearms Acquisition Certificate to firearms ownership, possession and use. This was contained in the original gun control legislation which was presented to Parliament before it was watered down.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH
speechtext:
That this House condemns the Government for its lack of consideration for Canada's youth, for its inaction in the face of the crisis an entire generation of Canadian men and women are faced with, and for neglecting to take immediate action in order to allow them to participate fully in Canadian society.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to the House today, at a time when the youth question has captured the attention of many Canadians but, unfortunately, has not sufficiently captured that of the Government. That is why we, the Official Opposition, want to dedicate this Opposition Day to making the Government and all Members of this House aware of the very serious situation we have in Canada today.
Mr. Speaker, at this very moment, there are 700,000 young Canadian men and women who, although they want to participate fully in society, unfortunately have no opportunity to do so. We have 700,000 young people who are asking society for a small place in the sun, who really want to work, and they are being told outright: Sorry, no room.
We have these 700,000 individuals who are losing all their illusions and who, in many cases, have already lost hope, because after the sacrifices they made to get an education, their hopes and dreams have now been dashed by the current situation and by the state of the economy. Today, I thought it was essential for the Government, and in this respect, I do deplore the absence of the Minister of State (Youth) (Mrs. Champagne). She seldom has an opportunity to take part in the proceedings, and she is probably waiting for someone to write her speech so she can rehearse it, like a script. Meanwhile, I am sorry she is not here in the House to discuss with us the problems of Canada's youth.
Mr. Speaker, I think all Canadian men and women will realize that we, as parliamentarians and with our responsibility for the well-being of Canadians, should ask ourselves a number of questions and do some soul-searching.
We should ask ourselves whether as elected representatives, we have done enough to make equal opportunity a reality for young Canadians. And if during the recession, we merely did what we could to save what we already had, we must remember that those who had nothing were unable to enter the system.
We should also ask ourselves whether we are parliamentarians and especially you as the Government have fulfilled the mandate you were given by Canadians. After looking at the statistics and reading various papers published by the Government, we realized that since September 4, 1984, when this
March 12, 1986

Government received a majority of support from young Canadians, they were the first group this Government decided to drop. And it did so for a very simple reason. This group does not have a powerful lobby. It is not one of Frank Moore's customers. It is not... in fact, it is isolated in so many ways, Mr. Speaker. And of course this Government is ignoring the isolated members of this group, each of whom is going through some particularly dramatic situation.
The Minister of State (Youth) has buried her head in the sand ever since her appointment. She would not face reality. She thought that she had been appointed to speak on behalf of all those who had succeeded, to strut about, to try and convince everybody that everything was fine and dandy in the best possible world, and to avoid at all cost to address the needy. As you know, Mr. Speaker, she has defended so weakly her constituency that she has been divested entirely of her own department and budget.
The Minister of State (Youth) is here today before us with the only support of her chauffeur and limousine. Under these circumstances, I do not think that she can do much for her constituency who need help so very much.
When we look at the situation straight in the face, Mr. Speaker, we realize that it is a tragedy. The unemployment level is very high and, as usual, the Prime Minister will provide us with a whole series of figures which the Minister of State (Youth) will repeat. But the whole situation is much more serious than these figures would indicate.
They say the unemployment level is lower than it was in September 1984, but youth unemployment increased last month, something nobody mentioned in the House. And the tendency is not downwards. I dare hope that the Minister of State (Youth) will realize for instance that in Nova Scotia, the unemployment level among young Canadians is .9 per cent higher than it was when she assumed her portfolio. It has also increased in New Brunswick since then.
It is all very nice to generalize, but there are particular situations. When we read the Nielsen report and realize that businessmen are now controlling this Government, we can imagine what is happening to the poor devils who are 16, 17 or 18 years of age. They cannot influence the Government. They are represented by a Minister who was supposed to defend them and, now that she is on her way out, can hardly defend herself. They have a Minister who wanted to manipulate them. Her own correspondance bears witness to that, Mr. Speaker. She is more interested in the future of the Federation of Young Conservatives than in the lot of young Canadians generally.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that it is scandalous for her to want to
spend $7.5 million of taxpayers' money to get young people to
join the Progressive Conservative Party-the Minister con-
Supply
fessed that much herself-while fully ignoring the dramatic situation of young Canadians generally.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State (Youth) confessed her helplessness in her letter dated January 6, 1986. She recognized having wasted $100 million in the Youth programs since her election. If this is being concerned about the situation of young Canadians and being part of a Government eager to meet their needs, Mr. Speaker, I cannot understand how the Minister of State (Youth) can claim today having done a good job over the past year and a half.
Mr. Speaker, looking back at what has been going on these last few days, there was, of course, that famous letter from the Minister, but there was also the spectacular, sad and dramatic gesture by our colleague from the Upper House, Senator Jacques Hebert. And that gesture, Mr. Speaker, is a symbol of how serious the situation is. This does not happen every day, and indeed I think it is the first time in history that a Member of this Parliament has decided to offer himself, his health in fact to try and wake up the bunch of sleepyheads in the Government.
Mr. Speaker, I see some of the Members shaking their heads. But I do not expect one single Member in that party to have the courage to defend a constituency with that much faith and devotion. And to that extent, Mr. Speaker, I feel the situation will force the Government to start thinking, because they have been laughing these last three days.
I venture to predict that their laugh will turn sour as days go by because they will have the whole situation on their conscience. And then, I think that over the coming days, the media will keep focusing the general public's attention on the situation of our young. All of us in our constituencies are aware of instances of neighbours, of people we know who have not found jobs, whatever the statistics may say. We know that the Manpower Centres are filled with young people waiting in line for opportunities.
It is therefore not good enough to be satisfied with the situation and refer to statistics. I do not understand why the Government does not admit its error now. They slashed through programs, in an arbitrary, hasty and somewhat vengeful way. But actually, it is not senator Hebert who is being hurt, but the thousands of young people who had pinned their hopes on that program. And the thousands of young people who are also waiting for the Government to respond to the Senate report.
In the Senate report, Mr. Speaker, there are 26 recommendations. It is not a Liberal report, it is a unanimous Senate report, about which Conservatives senators have agreed with Libera] senators to say this: The situation is far past the stage of partisan considerations. And although that report was made public, we did not even hear a whistle from the Minister of State (Youth), as usual. However, the other Members of the Governement should take the time to read it, and act on it

March 12, 1986
Supply
because what is in that report is a call from the heart, and it is my hope that this Government will have the courage to act within the shortest possible time. I suspect there is a move, I think that in the last few days they have been thinking. It started three days ago when the Deputy Prime Minister said: "We will do nothing, all we have been doing is very well done, hurrah for the statistics, and those who do not appear in the statistics, let them manage by themselves".
Yesterday, the Prime Minister sent this reply to Senator Hebert, and in his letter the Prime Minister admitted: I would be the first to recognize that much more should be done for the young. That having been said, I think there is a move. Today the Prime Minister, probably on the way out of his caucus, said that probably, by the end of the month, the Government would be announcing new programs for the young. It would therefore seem that he is beginning to see the light. The Minister of State said she was not aware of anything. This is no news to us, she has never been aware of anything since she has been there, Mr. Speaker. I think she should inquire from the Prime Minister because it could help her in her speech today and she would look better if she did not contradict the Prime Minister before the end of the debate. I think it is important to know that at 12:23 p.m., according to a Canadian Press report, the Prime Minister has said he will announce new programs before the end of the month. However, she may no longer be there and this is why he did not ask her advice. However, Mr. Speaker, I think we should go beyond the personal case of the Minister of State, because the Government will deal with it, but we should look after the young people. As a result of the situation in the Senate which no doubt will become embarrassing for the Government, I know of no Government who would face such a situation without doing a self-examination and taking action.
In that case, why should we wait? Indeed, we know that a mistake was made when programs were swiftly cut. They admit that they have not done enough, that new measures will be taken before the end of the month but why are they not acting now? I think it would be in the interests of young Canadians. When the Government killed Katimavik, they promised that the $20 million would be transferred to another program and, of course, the Minister of State did not know what kind of program it would be.
It would perhaps be proper now for the Minister of State to rise, to show some leadership and announce a new program which would end the human drama of certain young people throughout the country and would hopefully satisfy our colleague, senator Hebert. Since certain Members are making light of the situation in the Senate, I would like to ask them to reflect on an editorial in today's Le Droit:
The most sinister sniggering in the history of the House of Commons in Ottawa may have been heard on Monday. The whole venerable assembly of the representatives of the Canadian people once burst out laughing about the problem of battered women. When advised Monday about the fast of Senator
Jacques Hebert, who is asking for the Katimavik Program to be reestablished, the Conservative Members of Parliament did something even more ugly.
The editorial goes on to say that, by laughing at Jacques Hebert and his hunger strike to save Katimavik, which represents the only ray of hope for many young people, the sniggering Conservatives showed their simplemindedness, their absence of morality, or even their pleasure at a situation which is in fact quite disastrous. There is no other reason to react as they did. I dare hope that the Minister of State (Youth) and all her colleagues will reflect upon these words written by editorialist Johannes Martin Godbout. Today the House is wondering what we as parliamentarians might do for that important segment of our population. It is a starting point.
We will be told there is no money, think of the funds required and the deficit. How far can we go on hiding behind deficits and sacrificing an important part of a generation? How wrong can our priorities be when we can find $1 billion to bail out wealthy bank depositors and pretend there is nothing left to help the most dynamic forces in our society? As suggested in the editorial, I think it is a lack of ethics.
I know that this Conservative Government is not overly sensitive to the plight of young Canadians, except perhaps to offer them minor census jobs. My colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) gave us a good example today when he told us that, at the request of the Minister of State (Youth), the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Mclnnes) followed her advice and offered census jobs to young people, particularly those who belong to the Ottawa University Conservative club. I think measures of this nature are not worthy of a proud Government or of parliamentarians like our colleague from Valleyfield who, I know, has a lot more class than that and is aware that the future of youth is a matter of honour and that we should not belittle the problems experienced by the new generation.
I think that the Government is not offering them opportunities because it feels that those who are lucky enough will make out all right, but too bad about the others. The fact is that solutions are there, they have been proposed by various organizations.
We have had studies galore. The one example I would give is the First Chance program which could have met urgent needs. The Minister of State (Youth) may laugh her head off! What to expect? I think she has no sense of responsibility, because young people urgently need ready access to the labour market, they need practical experience. I would suggest that the First Chance program could have been one of many avenues open to them. Call it whatever you like, but do something!
I think that it is important for young Canadians to feel that
not only big business lobbies can influence this Government,
that not only large companies, such as the oil multinationals.
March 12, 1986



which have so much attention already, can catch the attention of the Government, but that ordinary people can do the same, that is those who cannot afford to attend weekend conventions or come to Ottawa to protest. I have been told: There are not that many youth organizations because there are no demonstrations on the Hill. Even coming here from Montreal or Toronto is too much to ask people who might have to live on $145 a month in welfare benefits. Would we want them to live on even less? I think that you only have to look at the facts to realize that there is a major problem.
I therefore hope that the events of the last few days and the daily problems facing many young people will convince our friends opposite to stop being concerned only by those who make large contributions to the Party and to take care of real people. I hope that they will show-and we already know that this is a big business Government-that this Government also has a heart, that it has courage and that it can admit that, because the Members opposite tried to go too fast in reducing the deficit, they forgot to take into account the human factor and to examine the type of situation in which 700,000 young people find themselves, they forgot to consider that these young people need at least the same opportunities as the other elements in our society.
There is now a difference of 6 per cent in the unemployment rate for young people and the rate for older Canadians. Some positive action must therefore be taken to help these people.
I do not see why this Government refuses to accept its responsibilities and I am convinced that the discussions that many Members opposite will have next weekend in their own constituency will give them pause and convince them to ask their caucus, their Leader and their Ministers to take more positive action in the coming weeks.
I trust that this will happen sooner than later and that the signs shown by the Prime Minister these last few days will lead to the implementation of a major program, not only knick-knacks, but something substantial, not just a political gesture to try not to lose face and show that something has been done, but a real program, a bold program, geared to the needs of young Canadians.
I am convinced that, should you take a poll-and you do that often enough-you would find that Canadians would be willing to make some sacrifices for the upcoming generation. I can say, right now, that all Canadians want to give young people a chance.
Ask your own conscience, look at your own children. Don't you want them to have the same opportunities you had? I am not asking for more than that. Give our young people the same opportunities you had when you were their age. Then, you will have a clear conscience, you will know you have done your best by giving them the programs they need to have the same opportunities you had.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre), because of his experience, has his speeches oozing with both honey and gall.
Mr. Speaker, it is very easy to take the young as hostages. It is very easy, for instance, and especially when the galleries are packed full, to say to those young people: "You know, boys and girls, they would rather help the banks than you". This is very simple, especially when reference is made to banks, and the Hon. Member opposite knows very well that the bank situation is not a situation we had been looking for, but we had an obligation to act.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member also said earlier that the young were "a multitude of solitudes". 1 am repeating his exact words. 1 do not believe that at all. They are not a multitude of solitudes, but rather, in view of the rates we are currently noting-and this is why I would like to ask my question in that direction-since unemployment rates are now declining, I do not think we should speak of a multitude of solitudes. Quite the opposite, studies show they now have the highest possible rate of dynamism.
I would simply like to ask my question which is threefold. In the Prime Minister's letter to which he was referring earlier, it is stated: "On September 4, 1984, the unemployment rate among the young aged 15 to 24 was 18.4 per cent, and it is now 16.4 per cent."
This is quoting from Statistics Canada, unless you think that Statistics Canada is wrong once again. However, Statistics Canada says so: there are 2 per cent less unemployment according to the seasonally adjusted statistics.
Second, over the 18 months since September 1984, 50,000 new jobs have been created for young people. This again is quoted from Statistics Canada. Third, between February,
1980,	and September, 1984, young Canadians have suffered the loss of 285,000 jobs. This again is taken from Statistics Canada.
Mr. Speaker, my hon. colleague opposite was also Minister for Youth. What did he do at the time?
I will repeat the figures. Mr. Speaker, from 1980 to 1985, I will give January figures, seasonally adjusted figures:
In 1980, the young unemployed rate was 13.1 per cent; in
1981,	it declined to 12.9 per cent; in 1982, it rose to 15.3 per cent; in 1983, it rose to 20.4 per cent; and in 1984, it decreased to 18.4 per cent. The rate came down to 17.5 per cent and now to 15.9 per cent. But what do you make of those figures? They are not the same.

That is something your damned statistics do not show. But stop burying your heads in the sand, as the Minister of State (Youth) is doing, and face reality. And reality commands you, for human dignity's sake, to act. That is what we are beseeching you to do. I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, but I, for one, cannot accept, when faced with this human tragedy, that the Government should try to hide reality behind a series of figures. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this Government is being accused of ignoring Canadian youth. This Government is being accused of failing to deal with what they insist on calling "the crisis of a generation", and finally, it is being accused of failing to take immediate steps to deal with problems that this Government inherited from an administration that spent money as if it were going out of style but failed to deal with any of the problems the country was facing.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH
speechtext: That's right.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH
speechtext:
It is therefore not surprising, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian people rebelled as energetically as they did on September 4, 1984. And that is why, Mr. Speaker, this Government wanted first of all to get rid of this cancer that is eating at each and everyone of us, but especially at our youth, the children of Canada.

What we hear from Opposition Members is single word "spend". They do not care about a baby born this very minute who has a mortgage of $8,000 on its tiny shoulders.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH
speechtext:
Oh, oh!
Supply

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH
speechtext:
They do not care about the deficit, the national debt, which was eradicating every chance that child had to a decent life, a life to which every Canadian is entitled.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, we are being told to spend, even if there are no worthwhile results in the long run. Spend just the same! Create jobs for a few weeks, just long enough to let people draw unemployment insurance benefits and then go on welfare, until they are back in the same old cycle.
Mr. Speaker, when the Opposition says this is what Canada's youth wants, it shows how far removed it is from reality. 1 really wonder when these people last had a worthwhile discussion with young people.
The Hon. Member for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre) referred earlier to those who made it, but who does he think he is? He is fine, he has done very well for himself. Mr. Speaker, he never had those problems, and he is too young to have children who did. In fact, I wonder when he last had a serious conversation with young people.
Mr. Speaker, when Opposition Members insist on lamenting the lot of what they refer to as the lost generation, they are not only showing their ignorance of reality but, and this is much worse, they are insulting a whole generation of young Canadians who are making every effort to survive, despite the disastrous consequences of those long years of Liberal Government.
Our youth is not-I repeat, not a lost generation. They are young men and women struggling through a Liberal created mess, out of which this Government is now leading them surely and effectively.
We are not taking immediate measures to help young people, Mr. Speaker? I have heard of the pot calling the kettle black, but this form of hypocrisy should not be allowed, neither in this House nor in the worst God forsaken street of this world.
What did the Liberals do between February, 1980 and September, 1984 when young people lost 285,000 jobs and when the rate of unemployment soared to 18.4 per cent? What did they do, Mr. Speaker? They kept on with their make-work projects which never helped anyone acquire a permanent, rewarding job, and they continued to increase our national debt.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH
speechtext: What about Katimavik?

What did we do, Mr. Speaker? Fifty thousand jobs were created in a mere few months. I have heard the Opposition scream that they were not all permanent jobs. Again, Opposition Members have shown their lack of knowledge of what is

Yes, many in what the Opposition called that lost generation want to study and work. Our young Canadians are not all a bunch of drug addicts, alcoholics and suicidal people.

speechtext:
We know that during these difficult times for our young people, especially between 1980 and 1984, many of them had to leave school. We have made some important decisions. Young people must be given a chance to get back into the labour force, to make something of their lives and plan for their future. That is why we are allocating some very substantial funding for youth. Within the Canadian Jobs Strategy alone, we have allocated $700 million or 37 per cent of the Department's budget. Speaking of labour market integration, we will be spending $210 million to help those seeking their first job.
Institutional training: $280 million. Challenge '86: a total of $210 million.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, all young people are eligible for the other components of our Canadian Jobs Strategy, programs that will total almost two billion dollars this year.
Challenge '86 is a program that young students appreciate because it gives them an opportunity to acquire the experience they need to obtain a permanent job.
In 1984, the Young Canada Works Program had a budget of $200,000 and created 65,000 jobs. Challenge '85, with a budget-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH
speechtext: $200 million.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH
speechtext:
Excuse me, $200 million, and 65,000 jobs.
Challenge '85, with a budget of $205 million, has created more
than 100,000 jobs, of which 67 per cent were directly related to the individual's career or course of study.
In 1986, Mr. Speaker, with the private sector participating we will create even more jobs. We expect 120,000 summer jobs will be created.
Those who are less fortunate, including drop-outs, will be able to attend training courses and at the same time acquire practical job experience. This should encourage them to either continue their education or at least get some professional training. And we are being accused, Mr. Speaker, of inertia vis-a-vis our young people!

As well, we have loans and loan guarantees that will be available for students, for those who would rather start their own business. This is how to encourage leadership and entrepreneurship. This is how to avoid condemning an entire generation to a lifetime of welfare.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH
speechtext: Come on.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH
speechtext: As the Quebec poet Felix Leclerc said so eloquently, Mr. Speaker: The best way to kill a man is to pay him to do nothing.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH
speechtext:
You have been doing that for twenty
years.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH
speechtext:
Because we are aware that too many people have to rely on welfare to live while looking for employment, an extra $100 million was directed to them in the Budget. This will also benefit a lot of young people.

In 1986, more than 200,000 young Canadians will benefit from federal employment programs, and this in addition to programs offered by Agriculture, CIDA, Indian Affairs and Northern Development, Fisheries & Oceans, Justice, Environment, and there are others, and of course the Department of the Secretary of State. And this Government does nothing for youth?
Mr. Speaker, because of the sad legacy of the previous Government, we have had to make some difficult decisions that will help put our finances in order. Katimavik is part of what the Prime Minister referred to as "painful measures".

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH
speechtext: Just to do the rich a favour.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it was impossible for a responsible Government to go on being so unfair to so many young Canadians. It was unthinkable to continue spending $20 million for the benefit of only 2,000 out of 4.5 million young Canadians who are entitled to take their place in society.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH

And 56 million to change the colours of the
uniforms.

speechtext: Katimavik was never meant to be a job-creation program, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH
speechtext: Right.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH
speechtext:
Its participants lived a great experience for nine months at a cost of $20 million a year. Was that fair, Mr. Speaker? Some of the participants even left school or a permanent job to get into the program. In the latter case they would get unemployment insurance benefits after. Was that fair? Considering the state of the country's finances, it became clear that the same money could be put to better use and, more important, directed toward a greater number of people.
I am quite aware that voluntary work can be most rewarding for whoever gets involved and for whoever is the beneficiary. During a recent of poll of young people between 15 and 24, some 24 per cent said they were currently doing volunteer or community work, and 73 per cent said that they would participate to acquire work experience. I am not surprised, because our young people are generous, kind, and wise. They want to help, and to help one another. The youth of Canada deserve better than to see 20 million of our scarce dollars shared by fewer than one-twentieth of one per cent of their peers.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps we should refresh the memory of our Liberal colleagues and remind them that about ten years ago, in one fell swoop, the Trudeau Government buried the Company of Young Canadians, ended all operations under the Opportunities for Youth program while slashing the Local Initiatives program budget by 30 per cent. All those programs were geared to young people. Those $77.5 million were ear-maked for something else, the equivalent of $200 million in current dollars. There was a resulting loss of 37,000 jobs. And now the Members of that same Party are sanctimoniously lecturing us about youth! Young people had to wait for nearly two years before Katimavik was launched. The Opposition applies a double standard, shamelessly.

Shamelessly they accuse us of throwing Canada's youth in Mr. Trudeau's "dire straights".

Mr. Speaker, at the Department of Youth we seriously consider reports from the Senate and the New Democratic Party. We carry out in-depth studies, as a responsible Government and a responsible Minister ought to do.
It is with sadness that I reflect upon the matter. If the Senators believed that the only really important thing in their report is that Katimavik is touted as having been the answer to all youth problems, then a lot of money has been wasted in drafting the report.
Supply

When one looks at the NDP report, the same word appears again, "spend". It is the flagship recommendation. They want us to spend $5,500 a year for two years for young people to do as they please; study, acquire skills, or simply think over what they might want to do when that money runs out. Mr. Speaker, $5,500 a year is not even enough for an ordinary Canadian, like the Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy), to take a decent holiday, as he stated recently. Like the song says, I wonder what the poor people do? This is not Camelot, this is Canada, and Canada is recuperating from 20 years of wasteful Liberal policy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH
speechtext:
Young people do not want a new form of welfare. They do not want to be part of a ghetto where, no matter what one does, he or she is considered a desperate, lazy, hopeless member of a lost generation.

Mr. Speaker, young Canadians spoke and our Government listened to them.
Young Canadians seek an opportunity to better themselves, they want to acquire the training and experience needed to secure lasting employment, work that will enable them to increase their knowledge and improve their standard of living. That is exactly what the Government has done. It showed concern, it has already acted and it will continue to act for the benefit of all groups and all regions. And, as the Prime Minister said, we will go even further when the time comes.
Mr. Speaker, rebuilding a country is somewhat like renovating a house. One must be sure that the foundation is on solid ground before spending money on decorations.
We are rebuilding this country with young people who day by day begin to feel hopeful again. First and foremost we must ensure that young people do have a future.

Politics becomes a very sad word when it is used to drown the hopes of a generation, when it is used to insult a generation which is but paying for the mistakes of the past, and when one is blackmailed into believing that life without any real personal responsibilities will cure all that may seem imperfect. Nobody said life was easy, but living it is worthwhile, but only if you keep on trying.
"Spend" they say. Yes, Mr. Speaker, we do, and we will, but wisely, and where it is most needed. That is what the Government will continue to do for Canada, for those who are very much part of our present, and for whom and with whom we are building tomorrow.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to the Minister for dealing at last with the unemployment situation with which young Canadians are faced, but I should like her to tell me . .. When she said that she had consulted young Canadians, maybe she was inferring that we had not consulted them enough. I know that over the past year, the Minister has spent $400,000 to organize regional meetings which were to culminate in a national conference supposedly to develop a national consensus on priorities for young Canadians. Now that she has renounced for the time being her project to hold her national conference, presumably for lack of funds, could she tell us what will happen of all her consultations? Will she publish a report? Did she hold consultations with young people just for the sake of making them talk? What I should like the Minister to tell us is whether the national conference will take place in two years, after the International Year of Youth, or does she intend to hold it very soon as promised?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have always indicated that the national conference would take place later, that the International Year was only a step towards better things and continued involvement with young Canadians. The International Year has been for all parties concerned a period of deep reflexion; it provided young people who had never been consulted an opportunity to express themselves. Previous Governments would set up and abandon programs without ever consulting young Canadians. Throughout this International Year, our Government has dialogued with young Canadians from all parts of Canada, from Newfoundland to the Yukon Territory. When the time comes to get young Canadians together again, we will do so, but at the time I, together with the Prime Minister, will choose, without the young people needing to wait for a decision from the Hon. Member for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre).

If I had wanted to arrange the figures, I would have quoted the second line for February when unemployment figures are always the highest. I would have done so if I had wanted to arrange the figures. I quoted the figures for January.
I said earlier that, in 1982, the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate was 15.3 per cent. I have the honour to inform you that, if I had wanted to arrange the figures, I would have announced a rate of 15.4 for February, 16.2 for March, 16.8 for April, 17.6, and normally, in July, when many young people have jobs, the rate is lower, but while the rate for January was 15.3, in July of the same year, it was 21.3. Mr. Speaker, I would like first to ask the Minister whether, in the said $11.7 billion she was referring to, family allowances are included, because I think those figures are misleading our people.
I would also like to ask her sincerely whether she is now saying, as mentioned by the Prime Minister, that the Government is ready to announce programs for the young. She knows very well that Senator Hebert is now on a hunger strike that could have truly serious consequences for his health.
I heard the Minister speak in good faith outside the House when she stated Senator Hebert was a man who represented a certain hope for the people. She spoke well of him outside the House.
If her Government is ready to announce something, why is she not doing it today, a program that would give some hope not only to Senator Hebert but to the young people? Because we know that in the Nielsen Report, where reference is made to Katimavik, it is said that if that program were cancelled without being replaced by another one, this could cause despair among young Canadians.
I think the Government's decision to kill a program which the Prime Minister himself (Mr. Mulroney) said was good, was made because this was a former Liberal program. It was not killed because it was a bad program, since it was a program recognized by the Canadian people and internationally as a program that provided the joy of living, training, life experience, quality of life to those who never had much luck in life.
Therefore, why? If she really represents the young in the Cabinet, why does she not react today and give a little hope to those young Canadians who are following the debate today and who ask for a single gesture today from the Government and the Minister that would give some hope to our young people?
As far as we are concerned, we do not call the young "junkies" or alcohol-prone. But it must be recognized that the suicide rate among young people has doubled over the last ten years. And we are now beginning to see that this may be a lost generation, a generation without hope.
As a woman, it seems to me that she can understand the plight of a generation without hope.
Why does she not give some hope to these people today through an announcement, whether it be only $20 million, or whether it is a step in the right direction for the Katimavik program? But at least let her send a signal to the young of our country.

Mr. Speaker, the end of Katimavik was announced by the Minister responsible for it a few weeks ago and the Government had then to make that decision, "a painful decision" as the Prime Minister said yesterday, considering the needs of young people, the lack of available funds

and especially the very small number of young people who could take advantage of the program.
Nobody ever said that the program was not satisfactory, that it had nothing good. We cannot at present give special privileges to a mere 2,000 young people when there are 4.5 million of them and we have so little money.
The Prime Minister said today:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to rise in support of the Liberal motion.
I listened to the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne) who berated us because we expected her to announce some new programs. I would have to assert that I had no such expectation. I do not expect the Minister of State to do very much more than she has already done, which is nothing. She also berated us for alleging that she was not concerned about youth. We know that she is concerned about youth because she devoted a full-length letter to her colleagues about this subject.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH
speechtext: Why is she leaving?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH
speechtext:
We would not expect the Minister of State for Youth to stay and listen to the debate about those people about whom she cares so much. She said that we did not acknowledge her concern for youth, but we were recently table to identify quite specifically her concern for youth. Her concern for youth is that they are a target of recruitment for the Progressive Conservative Party's youth federation. She alleged that we did not believe her concern about the problems of youth but we know that she is very much concerned about the problems of youth. Why else would she attempt to exploit the problems of youth to meet the ends of her own recruitment policy for which her office is being used?
We have just completed International Youth Year. Perhaps I should remind the House why International Youth Year was declared by the United Nations. As in the case of women, members of the United Nations believed that there should be a year for youth in order to focus attention on the imminent crisis that was affecting young people, particularly in the western world. Riots had already taken place and there was a great deal of concern that if something was not done about the unemployment among young people a crisis of significant proportions would lead to social disruption. International Youth Year was not intended to be a year of celebration for
the accomplishments of youth, as it was celebrated in Canada in many respects, but was intended specifically to focus attention upon the concerns, the problems and the need for participation by young people in determining policies that would affect their lives.
The Minister of State for Youth says that she has been consulting with young people. During International Youth Year her Ministry sponsored a number of forums. She attended these forums, leaving in her wake deep disappointment among many that she did not have the time to spare to sit down with young people to listen to their problems at length, as many of us have done.
They do not want to be told what problems to discuss or what their concerns should be, they simply want us to listen. These forums were rather consistent with the content of the Minister's letter and, in many instances, were seen by young people as attempts to steer the discussion of youth toward directions chosen by her Party in order to support her philosophies and those of her Party. Therefore, perhaps it is not a great disappointment that the fifth national forum has been cancelled after four which served little purpose for young people. Perhaps we must admit that a fifth forum would have served little purpose.
Until recently the International Youth Year failed in its goal to provide a focus on the concerns of youth. I was involved as critic for youth and post-secondary education in the New Democratic task force which coursed across the country and talked to hundreds of young people. There are so many easily identifiable problems affecting so many youth that I believed that the media and the three Parties in this House would have been able to respond. I have been puzzled, grieved and saddened by the great difficulty in drawing attention to the plight of young people in this country.
When I say that some 25 per cent of the population of young people represent a lost generation, I am not denying the contribution, the honesty and creativity of young people. However, when we consider how the problems of many young people are being disregarded and reflect upon why there is the rejection of effective participation by youth, I recall the many graduation speeches I have heard in which adults have told young people: "Tomorrow this will be your world because you are the leaders of tomorrow".
Let us examine the background of such statements. It means that this is our world today but will soon belong to young people. We are saying that eventually someone will take over our territory and we will have to concede to youth. Perhaps when we tell youth that this will be their world tomorrow and they will be tomorrow's leaders we are really confessing that we are suspicious of our youth and do not want them to be involved because they are the enemy. I believe we must stop projecting that attitude in our relationship with young people and begin to consider youth as our partners in this democracy, from whom we have much to gain in developing the destiny of this country.
We have also heard the assertion that today's youth are
going through the same experience we had when we were
March 12, 1986

young. This is not true. Our experience as youth in this country and throughout the world was quite different from today's youth. Many of us earned our political spurs in the 1960s. While many of us participated in social actions that could have caused us trouble, we knew we would ultimately be able to get a job. Indeed, some may ultimately end up in the Parliament of Canada after engaging in near revolutionary movements. In those days there was full employment but today there are many young people who are unemployed and may never have a job.
Today's young people are awash in information. They have received far more information in half an hour of television than they can learn from a week in the classroom. At no time in history has a population grown up in circumstances where change is so rapid with respect to technology, the transfer and the flow of information that there is little time to prepare or make judgments.
We did not grow up in communities where families were subject to such dramatic and drastic change. Many young people are the children of single parents and come from families that suffered marriage breakdown. Today, family relatives live far apart. The atmosphere among families today is one in which they spend six minutes a day to discuss family concerns.
There is a vast difference between now and then. That is why the young people of today are pleading for more help, more advice and more guidance. There were recommendations that there be significant changes in the educational system because the youth of today are different. They are different because of the environment in which they grow up. Their needs are substantially different. Their experience and problems are different. So we had better stop looking at young people through a distorted mirror. We must see them through a window which reveals their lives. We should try to understand their particular experience of growing up in this world.
I must confess to a certain degree of gratitude. Over the last few weeks, the release of the New Democratic Party task force report, the Senate committee task force report, the ineptitude, unfortunate as it may be, of a Minister who was caught in serious error and, now, more recently, the grievance expressed in the form of a hunger strike by an eminent Senator, have all brought some focus on the problems of our youth. I hope that this emphasis on young people will not be aborted. I have been very much concerned about the lack of attention given to the youth of Canada in this House. Although I believe it is unfortunate that a hunger strike by one of its own has brought the Liberal Party more consciously into the effort, I appreciate that it is with us. I hope that the Conservatives will begin to realize that what we are talking about is not a share of already existing programs but rather the initiatives which will be taken in response to what has been identified by two task forces, and many others, as a unique problem.
Let us consider the Senate report and our own report. Let us look at the recommendations in contrast to what we have been
Supply
hearing from the other side. There are two things on which both reports agree, first, that the problem of youth is significant and we should address their needs as unique and not relating to the rest of the population; and second, and this is by far the most important, that there must be some means by which young people can be involved in advising all levels of Government of their needs and concerns. We should provide youth with the means of participation in a variety of ways. One of these would be to ensure the existence of youth advisory councils at both the federal and the provincial levels. Youth chosen by democratic means could be given the opportunity, through the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne), who is supposed to be a true advocate for youth, to advise Government and Government Departments of their needs and concerns. We should enhance the opportunities for young people to be heard from on all of the issues affecting them.
Our task force report made a number of recommendations.
[ Translation]
The goal of the task force was to provide a forum for young people and alow them to speak about the various Government policies which affect them, to state their views on various social, economic and political issues and to promote the development of new strategies to meet economic needs as far as social development was concerned and this involved over 4 million young Canadians aged 15 to 24.

One of our important recommendations was with respect to youth prospects. We do not mean a hand-out like the $2.8 billion for the research and development credit. It is not like the capital gains exemption. It is not a hand-out like the money which went to the banks and which benefited the banks outside our borders to the extent of 30 per cent. None of these things were subject to the criticism that those people would waste the money on vacations, cars, and so. In fact, one got the impression that if they did go on vacations and purchased cars, it was probably a good thing to do with the money.
Our recommendation was intended to provide opportunity. We were impressed by the fact that, to a large extent-as a result of the inaction of the Government in respect of the financing of universities-accessibility to universities was being seriously impeded. The gains which had been made in the last decade in providing opportunities for minorities, the disabled and women were being restricted as a result of financial exigency by the Government. It failed to respond to the needs of the universities in a number of respects. We have encountered many young people from poor families who, were they to go to university, would incur debts totalling as much as $40,000. They would be faced with nine years or ten years of making payments at the rate of $350 a month. We also found that the youth from poor families could get an allowance if they went into a training program. So we have an arrangement that creates an essential bias. The poor go into the training programs and the rich go to university.

March 12, 1986
Supply
There were a number of other problems which existed among young people which had to be addressed in an effective way. We suggested a program which would affect young people between the ages of 18 and 22 years. If they chose to participate in the Youth Prospects Program, then they would be provided not with a gift of $5,500, but with an allowance just like the allowances which are provided for training programs now and which are denied those young people going to college and university. This will make it possible for young people of all classes and all backgrounds to make a reasonable choice of whether to go to university or college or to go into entrepreneurship programs or work skill developments which are similar to Katimavik, or to go into industrial training programs which exist now. Such a program, if integrated with already existing programs at the federal and provincial levels will cost relatively little. It would certainly cost a good deal less than the $30 billion in deferred taxes afforded to large corporations. It would cost less than the $11 billion in tax expenditures which benefit the larger corporations. Indeed, it would cost exactly the same amount of money as the capital gais exemption and at its peak would cost no more than $1.4 billion.
It disturbs me, as I am sure it disturbs many of the young people from whom I have heard-who regard this as an excellent program in response to their needs-that the Government would criticize such a program on the basis of cost at the same time that it shows such quick generosity to the banks and large corporations. Moments ago we heard that $1 billion was given to the banks because of the urgency. The problem of youth is far more urgent than the problem of those who had the stupidity to take a chance and who expected the Government to bail them out.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that it has become all too rare for the House of Commons to focus its attention, at least for a while, on the problems of Canada's youth. Therefore, I wish to commend most heartily my hon. friend and colleague, the Hon. Member for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre), who has brought forward today this very important motion which gives us the opportunity to reflect on the difficulties being faced by a very major segment of our society. I do not believe the motion which is before us today really calls for very much in the way of partisan exchange. What it does call for is the need for some concerted action. It is to that issue I would like to address my remarks.
I wonder how many Members of Parliament there are who are faced every week with the necessity of signing scores of letters which state something like this:
This will acknowledge receipt of a copy of your resume.
While your qualifications are certainly of interest and your curriculum vitae is impressive, there are at present no openings in my office. Your name, however, will be kept on file.
1 regret that my response must be negative. Please accept my best wishes for success as you seek suitable employment.
I wonder how many companies, firms, businesses and industries-employers generally-there are who have to sign letters similar to that every week. I am sure the people who sign those letters do not feel good about it. It is simply a fact of Canadian life since youth unemployment today in Canada is really of tragic proportions. I do not think it is being too dramatic when I say it is a crisis-it is a crisis. The unemployment rate was nearly 17 per cent throughout 1985. That is distressing beyond words. But it does not do any good, as I have heard earlier today, to throw back and forth statistics. We know that if the situation is improving at all it is only marginally, and then the statistics themselves may be false. I will come back to that point in a moment.
What are these cold statistics? Let us translate them into human reality and determine for a moment what they mean. In part, they mean lower self-esteem. I have been to youth conferences, some conducted in my own constituency. I have spoken with young people on the streets of the towns and villages which I represent. A lower sense of self-esteem is evident among the youth to whom I have spoken. I have been witness to social alienation because of youth unemployment, family conflicts, a dissatisfaction with one's own existence, a
Supply
feeling of having no control over one's life, and, of course, one cannot fail to mention individual hardship. If one does not have the wherewithal for decent shelter and adequate nutrition, then there is personal physical hardship. There are some in our society who are much more affected than others. I wish to take just a moment to refer to native youth.
In the report of the Senate committee which was chaired by Senator Jacques Hebert, reference is made to the fact that native young people often try to escape their seemingly hopeless prospects. That was brought home to me today when I received a news report from the Province of Alberta indicating that three people from Peerless Lake in northern Alberta died yesterday. These people drank a mixture of Lysol and fluid from a photocopying machine. Six other people also drank the mixture. All were in the age group of 16 to 34. Doctors in an Edmonton hospital are now fighting for the lives of the survivors.
Peerless Lake is a poor and very isolated community of about 300 people, mainly Cree Indians. It is not a modern, urban area. The community leader-and this is the point of my bringing this to your attention, Mr. Speaker-said that it was just a matter of time before such a tragedy struck because, according to him, only one in seven persons in that community has a job. He says that there is no future for the young people there. He said that they are lost and are desperately looking for an escape. That is why I have said that the figure of 17 per cent for youth unemployment is a false one.
There are many thousands of young people in society who have simply given up on the futile effort of job hunting. Native people are not even included in the statistics provided by Statistics Canada. We all know that young people are usually the very last to be hired and that when there is some reason to slow down the operation of a plant or a business, they are the first to be fired. What many of them know best today is part-time jobs, minimum wages, unemployment insurance benefits if they can qualify or very often just simply nothing at all.
Canada and most of its western trading partners have been through quite a terrible recession. We are just now beginning to emerge out of the dark tunnel of economic downturn. For that we are grateful. For many in Canada, the situation is somewhat better than it was before and the future does look a little brighter, or at least it did before the recent Budget, and I am concerned that that Budget may have a very dampening effect on our fragile economic recovery. However, for hundreds of thousands of Canadian young people, there is as yet no sign at all of hope.
The Senate committee on youth stated that although young people are called the lost generation, they could still be saved through swift, vigorous initiative. Today's motion is calling for some swift, vigorous initiatives. We want government action to be focused on this problem. However, so far the Government has not done that much to assist the economic recovery. Whatever it has done has certainly not assisted youth. I do not
11478

March 12, 1986
Supply
hear very many young people saying: "Let the good times roll".
If we had to describe the age in which we live, and it is very difficult to do because we live right in the midst of it, perhaps we could describe this as being the age of human rights. We now have a Charter of Rights and Freedoms which is part of the Constitution of Canada. A report entitled Equality for All has just been tabled in the House of Commons. There is a great deal of emphasis on human rights and equality. Nevertheless, despite these endeavours, there is serious discrimination against a major segment of society, and that is youth. Young people are being discriminated against.
A witness who appeared before the Senate youth committee had this to say:
Youth are . . . discriminated against when it comes to giving them the opportunity to make it on their own. When applying for venture capital, youth are discriminated against because of their age and inexperience. What is needed is a change of attitude toward young people who want to take the initiative in changing their lives.
That is very telling testimony. In my view, that is what is needed, but here is what we have. We have instead a professor from the University of Regina who said before that same committee the following:
-many of the young people out of work today will be unable to find a job during their lifetime-
It should, therefore, come as no surprise to any of us in the House that there are many persons in society today who are feeling a sense of panic and despair regarding young people. These persons include parents, teachers, community workers, church ministers and priests, social workers, medical doctors and many others. Many young people in society are looking around them and seeing no doors opened. They are seeing no way to escape from their present situation. Did you know, Mr. Speaker, that one of the definitions of hell is no exit?
What we need at the federal level today is a strong and very effective Minister of Youth. If the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) could be made aware by Members of Parliament of how serious and urgent the situation is and that it is a crisis, he would choose from his frontbench the best and make him or her responsible for youth programs, both existing ones and new ones. Maybe he would reach into the backbenches for the most talented of the newcomers to Parliament and say: "We are giving you that responsibility and we are going to back you up because the Government has got to do something for the young people of Canada".
We need programs like Katimavik, First Chance, the Youth Jobs Strategy and many, many others. I do not want to harp incessantly on Katimavik, but I think it was a good program. The residents of a home for the aged called North Centennial Manor wrote me a letter to say the following:
We are taking this opportunity to express our support for Katimavik, the federally-funded youth program which has enhanced the life of our residents.
We ask that the Government reconsider its decision to end the Katimavik program which has proven to be a worth-while educational learning experience to the youth of our nation.
The letter goes on:
Katimavik is a positive, enriching experience which demands the best out of young people. We need Katimavik to give our youth the chance to learn, to live and to work.
We need programs like that and we need many others besides.
We in this Party recognize that there has to be fiscal responsibility. We recognize that when the deficit was incurred in Canada, we were in a recession and we had to soften the terrible impacts of that recession. We recognize that, but now we are beginning to recover and we need economics of recovery. We have to enlarge opportunities for young people so that they may work in and serve the society in which they live.
The Senate report on youth directed its recommendations toward Governments. It did not say that Governments can be excused and that we must look to the private sector or we have to look outside the country or anywhere else. The recommendations are directed to Governments, both federal and provincial, and they say that Governments should recognize their respective areas of jurisdiction and accept their responsibilities by joining efforts to fulfil a common objective.
Dealing with the situation of youth in the 1980s must be done without any more delay, and it must be done by every means possible. It should be known by the House of Commons that 81 per cent of the young people in our society who have jobs today have expressed satisfaction with the work they are doing. When those without work are questioned, they have given having a job as their highest priority. There is a message for us. If we simply regard youth as being the casualties of an economic system, then there can be no spur to action.
The Senate committee indicated that instead of waiting for improvement in the economy to reduce unemployment, we should reduce unemployment to improve the economy. That is my kind of economics. It is the new economics which says that job-creation is not a cost to Government. It is not only an outlay or an expenditure; it is a stimulus for renewal and for economic recovery.
I conclude by saying that what this Opposition Day is all about can simply be stated by referring once more to the excellent Senate report entitled Youth: A Plan of Action, as follows:
Despite the economic recession from which we have barely recovered, Canada is one of the richest countries in the world. We have at our disposal the means by which to help our young people. The public and political will to remedy the situation must be displayed without further delay. Each Canadian community must assume control of its own affairs and put its imagination to work so that we may improve the present and future lives of our young people. Just as in the event of a major national disaster, we as Canadians must concentrate all our energy to solve this serious problem.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great attention to the comments of the Hon. Member. I have a great deal of respect for the Hon. Member, and it is because of that that I was most interested in what he had to say. In addition, as a father myself with two daughters, one of whom is about to graduate this year from university, a daughter who has no job
March 12, 1986

at the moment, a daughter who has tried until now to find a job for herself for after graduation, I understand the concerns about which the Hon. Member spoke from personal experience. However, 1 want to tell him that four years ago, when I served as the mayor of one of the six municipalities in Metropolitan Toronto and served on Metropolitan Toronto Council, I was appointed to head a task force on youth unemployment. The task force was set up specifically at a time when youth unemployment was astronomically high. It was set up at a time when there were problems generally with unemployment for youth, particularly with that portion of the youth population who were school drop-outs, who had difficulty understanding how to make application for a job, who had difficulty knowing how to dress properly when they went to a job interview, and who had difficulty getting up in the morning to go to the job once they had one. The task force was set up to try to get around or deal with those types of problems. We set up a program and we approached all levels of Government for some financial assistance. At that time we found great difficulties in obtaining help from the federal Government of which the Hon. Member was a supporter and sat in the House supporting.
In August, 1982, I led a delegation from Metropolitan Toronto to Ottawa to see the then Minister of Employment and Immigration who continues to sit in the House, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy). We came to him and we put our case on the table. The Hon. Minister at that time was very sympathetic. He indicated to us that he understood our concerns and that he wanted to get immediate action. That was at the beginning of a week. He turned to his assistant and he told his assistant to go down to Toronto on the Friday, solve the problem on which we wanted an answer and get the thing on the rails.
I left office as a mayor in November, 1982, to run for Parliament because at that time there had not been any action as a result of my pleas to the Minister and to the former Government on the whole question of youth unemployment. I ran for Parliament and was elected in September, 1984, as the Hon. Member knows. Two years had passed since I had been up to Ottawa before the then Government, and there was still no action.
I understand what the Hon. Member is saying and I know that he understands. Notwithstanding his comment, his concerns go back a long way. They do not start in September, 1984. His concerns go back to the days when he was a member of the governing Party and the problem was shaping up, being created and going on to be a dramatic and desperate problem in the country.
I know the Hon. Member is a sincere Member, so I should like to ask him a question. What would he and his Party do differently today? The Liberals had a chance for 20 years to make sure that the problem did not happen. Once the problem had occurred, they had a chance to solve it. They had a chance for three or four years when the problem was very severe. Only 18 months has passed, but the Hon. Member has been stating this afternoon that things should be different and that differ-

ent things should be done. I assume that if his Party were in power again, different things would be done. 1 would sincerely like to know what is the specific policy of the Liberal Party in respect of youth unemployment today. What specifically would it do aside from reinstating Katimavik?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member gave me a great deal of help in answering the question. He is quite correct in saying that over a very long period of time I have seen Governments, different administrations following different elections, respond to a wide range of problems including the problem of youth unemployment. During a number of Liberal administrations over the time I have been here, 1 saw a very creative approach to programs for young people. They were very creative; sometimes they were too creative. I can remember when the Secretary of State announced some of those programs, and I recall the days when youth unemployment was nothing compared to what it is now. For example, a program was brought in known as Opportunities for Youth which went wild in many places. I remember members of the Opposition screaming about how government money was being ill spent on some of those projects. I investigated a few of them myself, called a halt to them and found myself in trouble with the then Secretary of State. However, those programs were modified.
The thing which impressed me about the Liberal administration is that they had a creative approach to the youth situation, and I think young people recognize that. What happened in the latter days of the last Liberal administration is that we were hit with a serious recession. It was not caused by that Government. That Government tried to counteract it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member referred to the world-wide recession. Of course, that is quite correct. There was a world-wide recession a few years ago but, as the Hon. Member is aware, it was much more severe in Canada than it was in virtually every other industrialized country in the western world. In my view and in the view of most, that was because of the specific types of policies followed by the Government of which he was a member, including the high interest policy, the National Energy Program and things of that sort. That is why youth unemployment in those years reached pretty close to 20 per cent.
Since the present Government has taken office, while no one is suggesting the problem is solved, there has been a drop in youth unemployment. The situation is not perfect as yet by any manner or means, but I think the Hon. Member will admit that the economic climate created by the Government since it took office has been of assistance in helping to get our youth back to work and to get the unemployment rates down.
Having said all that, Mr. Speaker, I heard the Hon. Member talk about what he thought in general terms the Government should do. I had asked him specifically what the policy was of the Liberal Party with respect to youth unemployment. Are there some specific programs which the Liberal Party would institute if it were the Government today? I would like to hear what they are.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the things I would not do, facing the situation we have at present, is to have cut-backs in youth programs, and that is what we have had. This is not the time for cutting back, but for recognizing that we have a serious problem.
Even with a deficit reduction program in effect across the board, I think the Hon. Member who raised the question will have to recognize that there have to be some exceptions. We have a segment of our society that is suffering to a greater extent than other sectors. Our young people are not participating in the recovery and they need special attention. There should not be cut-backs.
We need Government job-creation programs of a variety. A lot of thinking has been going on with respect to the kinds of programs that can be initiated. Attention should be given to them until our young people are able to participate in the recovery and until the situation is no longer fragile. They can
then get into the real world of work and we will no longer need Government job-creation programs.
The Member is on very slippery ground when he begins to analyse statistics and says things are getting better. I doubt whether the throwing of statistics by Members at each other will convince a single young person that the situation is getting better. There is a crisis. To argue about a point and a half or two points, knowing the statistics are probably false anyway, is not very helpful.
I cannot sit down without reminding the Hon. Member, who had to throw in the National Energy Program, that perhaps the Tories would like to have some aspects of that program alive and well today in western Canada-
