subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to speak on the motion today. I believe the Government's record is an enviable one, enviable because everybody on the benches opposite would like to be in that position. They may have a little trouble admitting it, but I really believe that is true.
I think it is important to mention a little bit about my background as my colleague, the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) has done. I have spent a lifetime working on a daily basis with the youth, as a high school principal concerned with their future and their education. There is no question that over this 25 year period I have seen a tremendous increase in the fears and worries of young people as to what part and what role they will play in our future.
In the mid-1970s youth unemployment was probably first recognized. By 1984 there had been 100 per cent increase in youth unemployment from the mid-1970s, and it was then recognized as a major problem in Canadian society. I think also it is important to see what people in educational and youth roles were thinking in the mid-1970s and the early 1980s.
I can recall representing a rather large group of my former colleagues before the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) who was a Minister in the previous Liberal Government. I can remember, as my colleague from York East did, trying to implore the Minister at that time to make some changes on behalf of our youth. Today the words used were "swift, vigorous action". We tried to get that in the mid-1980s as youth unemployment soared, but the words fell on deaf ears. Nothing happened except that it motivated a few of us to get into politics.
Since 1984, the Government has chosen the right course. There are, however, many things I would like to say today to set the record straight. Dramatic steps have been taken since September, 1984 on behalf of the youth, and they should hear about them here first.
March 12, 1986

We are now coming to the time of opportunities for young people to be in the workplace during their summer recess. It is a very important time for them, so let me begin by talking about it.
We have the Challenge Program in place. Challenge '85 last year was the first, and we are well ready for Challenge '86 this year. I think Members opposite are having difficulty understanding the fundamental difference that our Government sees in the philosophical development of young people and in preparing them for their future in the world of work.
In the late 1970s and the early 1980s our young people in school were wondering about the value of their education, how realistic it was and how it was tailored to the world of work which was surely to follow. They were having serious doubts about that education.
What role was the federal Government playing in all of this? When those doubts became apparent and submission after submission were made to the various Ministers in the previous Government, what were the young people being told? What solutions was the Government of the day coming up with? As unemployment soared to 18.4 per cent and seemed to be going out of sight, the country, and particularly the youth, demanded a new Government and a new focus.
Let us examine some of the things the young wanted and see whether the Government has them in place today.
First, we talk about the need in the late 1970s and early 1980s for work experience, the fact that young people have to have some opportunities in the real world to find out what work is all about in order to make better career choices and to develop their educational plans for their future. That was a very important statement in the late 1970s and early 1980s right across the country. What has our Government done about that? I think it is very clear. First and foremost and built right into the philosophy of the Challenge programs is the opportunity to provide of real life experiences for students while they are still in school, Mr. Speaker. They must be tied into their educational package. Therefore, the Government has tailored the Challenge program to work with the businesses and workplaces in Canada which have been encouraged to work with students and the Government to develop those opportunities.
The figures from 1985, which is the first year for which we can report anything, indicate that, in spite of a late start, we improved the rate of summer jobs for young people by 100,000. That is quite an increase. Not only did the number of jobs increase, but so did the quality of the experience. For the first time in the many years in which it has been traced, we found a dramatic growth in the involvement of the private sector in giving students jobs. That involvement jumped to 25 per cent in 1985, which is very significant because that is where the real jobs will be found upon graduation. That is where the real future of the country is. Almost 600,000 jobs have been created, the majority of them in small business in the private sector, which is exactly where we target these work experiences. It is very important to see the philosophy working.
Supply
I want young Canadians to know that the Government cares and has tied that in.
I have taken a personal survey of over 400 businesses in my riding. I asked about their involvement and how they feel about Challenge 85 and the potential for Challenge 86. Eighty-five per cent of those polled said they want to be involved in Challenge 86, which is again a very significant increase. In London, 1,200 businesses have come forward which want to be involved in providing young people with these opportunities. There has been a tremendous increase in the interest expressed in aiding young Canadians while they are still in the educational process. That is a very significant change from how the previous Government looked upon youth and youth development.
As a former educator I listened to stories of woe from many young people during the 1970s and early 1980s about the lack of opportunity and teachers who, in the views of the students, were out of tune with the educational requirements of the day. It became apparent that the Government had to show some leadership in the on-going education of young Canadians in the schools. Co-operative education provided that key. While still at school, young people were afforded the opportunity, for extended periods of time, to pursue an avenue of work experience, a slice of the reality of life. With that opportunity they can grow even further and make even wiser choices about their futures.
Since we took office we have seen tremendous financial growth in this area. In one year the figure has gone from $1.89 million to $2.86 million. Those are dollars well spent. We have been able to increase the number of participating school boards, universities, and colleges over tenfold. Even further increases are possible in the future which will help young Canadians make those critical decisions. I think we have underestimated the importance of this.
Another statistic which is vital to every educator in Canada is the drop-out rate. About 250,000 young people every year, for one reason or another, become disenchanted with our educational system and leave prior to graduation. These young people are at a tremendous disadvantage in the working world. We must find ways of keeping them in the educational system so that they will become better qualified to handle the demands of Canada's productive workforce.
I think we have started to find some of the answers. We realize that the problem exists and will not go away. Within the Canadian Jobs Strategy we have developed the Job Entry Program. This provides the opportunity for hundreds and hundreds of young people to get their first experience in the workforce, which is so important to a young Canadian. The experience they gain from an employer and the opportunities they have to speak with workers in the real world will influence them. It will provide the counselling and guidance which so many of our young people need. The Job Entry Program is now providing that opportunity.
It is only because we have tied our philosophical development into businesses and encouraged their participation that

March 12, 1986
Supply
any of this will work and affect our young people. It is important that people understand that. The Job Entry Program is geared specifically for young people who have never had a job and find themselves very much disadvantaged in the workplace and in society. Our workplace is very demanding today. Our cost of productivity must be lowered so that Canada can be competitive nationally and internationally. Our youth will best learn that lesson in the workplace and must have the opportunity to work in the private sector to get that opportunity.
Members opposite should try to assimilate that working philosophy. They should try not to be antagonistic to free enterprise and the private sector. I ask them to go home to their ridings and take a realistic look at the Canadian Jobs Strategy to see whether it will give tremendous opportunities to young people. I dare say that it will.
I do not think it need end there. One could go on and on listing real life examples of how the Job Entry Program has helped various young people, disabled groups, and young female workers trying to enter the workforce. Throughout the ridings of Canada one can see good and positive examples of that. In London there are 13 job entry projects on stream with over 320 young people getting their first opportunity to work. I have visited those projects and talked to the young people. From listening to them and watching them work I know they are getting experience which was not available in the past and which will help them to be of service in the future to another employer. I ask my colleagues to visit projects under the Canadian Jobs Strategy and see how it can enrich the lives of young people in their ridings.
[DOT] (W30)
There are other avenues for reaching not just the youth but the other unemployed and disadvantaged. Quite often we might find ourselves working with an entire family of unemployed. We work with the mother, father and the children, trying to get them to take an active role. We know how hard it is. This program, with its philosophical roots in the dynamics of our work structure, really cannot go wrong. There have been no cut-backs here. It has been very efficient.
At the start of my remarks I talked about the Challenge '85 and Challenge '86 programs. In my area alone we saw an expenditure of approximately $2.9 million. It was down this year to $2.6 million. At first one might tend to get angry about that. However, I am not at all angry because of the increase in the private sector's involvement. That meant a decrease in cost and we will get more summer jobs in that riding for less money than last year. That is what this Government is all about: Efficiency and a whole new way of doing things. That is what Progressive Conservatives stand for. As I said, that is what propelled me into this life.
One of the most exciting things for Members opposite to stop and consider is the innovation theme of the Canadian Jobs Strategy. This represents nothing but pure opportunity to create solutions to problems. The Liberals were asked today how they would solve this problem for young people. How
would they more quickly lower the unemployment rate? They were hard-pressed to give us any new solutions. I say that the road is through innovation. Go to your ridings and put this program to work. The Minister would like to hear about that. I have found the Department and the Minister most helpful.
The people in London-Middlesex, and I am sure this is true in many ridings across Canada, are as concerned about youth unemployment as anyone else. They have banded together and come up with some solutions to the problem. They have come up with an action plan, a new way to help young people. It has been said today that the plight in which young people find themselves could cause severe disruptions and alienation among youth. There has been criticism of our Government on this issue. Yet the people in London-Middlesex took on the challenge of innovation. They have worked hard and seriously with me on this issue. I hope and expect that I will stand in my place in a month or so and announce some very forwardlooking innovations which will help Canadian youth get the kind of career advice they need to stay in the mainstream of Canadian life. They will learn about themselves, their country, the world of work, and how they can participate. I say to my colleagues that if they look in their own ridings I am sure they will find great solutions to the problem of helping young people. We all know that they are our future and with their help Canada will become the country of the 21st century.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-ALLEGED LACK OF GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION FOR YOUTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege for me today to speak to the motion presented by the Official Opposition. First of all, I would like to make it clear to the House that I regret this motion is necessary. Although I welcome this opportunity to speak, I am sorry it should be necessary for the Opposition parties to speak to the situation in which Canada's youth finds itself today.
Mr. Speaker, in speaking to the subject of this motion, I would like to say first of all that I am glad this motion is couched in general terms, so that it gives us an opportunity to analyze the youth situation, not just from the employment point of view, although this is one of youth's priorities, but also because it gives us a chance to look at other questions that are equally relevant.
Mr. Speaker, for Canadians or for any nation in the world for that matter, youth is one of the most important times of our lives. When we are young, we form habits that will serve us during the rest of our lives, we develop our attitudes, our opinions and in a democratic society, even our political affiliations. It is in this season of our lives that the individual's potential is most obvious, but it is also a time when the gap between the individual's potential and what the individual can accomplish is greatest. Mr. Speaker, we must realize that even if our potential is at a very high level when we are young, our chances of achieving something with that potential are surrounded by all kinds of obstacles, owing to the fact that when we are young, we are still in our formative years and must still
March 12, 1986

go through a process of education and training. This means it is when we are young that we are most susceptible to the influence of others, including the influence of the State, the Government, the political environment in which we grow up and start to explore the world to which we belong.
Mr. Speaker, in discussing the general situation in which Canadian young people find themselves today, I would like to emphasize the role of employment in the lives of our young people. Getting a job is probably one of the highest priorities of most young people in this country.
However, Mr. Speaker, there are other priorities to be considered and analyzed in this debate. I am thinking of education: the education of the individual and the education that individual acquires by being a part of the Canadian community. There is also the future: What kind of future are we building for our children, for the children of our fellow citizens, for the children who tomorrow will be the youth of Canada, and for the youth which tomorrow will be the adults, the citizens, the voters of this country?
There is also the matter of welfare, and I am thinking not only of the very specific connotation of social assistance programs for the unemployed but also of the other sense of the word, the welfare of the individual.
Mr. Speaker, there is also the question of leisure and culture peculiar to an individual, either an ethnic culture, or a native culture, or let us say a strictly Canadian culture, an integrated culture or, as one might say without negative connotation, an assimilated culture.
Now then, Mr. Speaker, priorities can be found in the major actions, the major measures, the major policies of a Government. The attitude of a Government towards the young people of this country, today's specific issue, can really be found in Budget measures, in white or green papers, in major studies published and endorsed by a Government, in its policies.
With that in mind, Mr. Speaker, I would like to review some of the measures taken by this Government since it came into office 18 months ago, namely cut-backs and, unfortunately, financial restraints which force us to reduce rather than improve the type and quality of opportunities we can now offer to young Canadians.
Among others, Mr. Speaker, the reduction of transfer payments to the provinces for post-secondary education. Apparently, Mr. Speaker, the Budget restraints implemented by this Government mean that, between now and 1990, there will be a cut-back of $1.5 billion in the amount originally proposed.
Then, Mr. Speaker, the elimination of the Katimavik program.
As a former mayor who was once in a position to launch a Katimavik program in his community, as a former Indian Affairs and Northern Development district manager who could have encouraged native communities to implement programs like Katimavik, Mr. Speaker, I consider this a tragic
Supply
loss because so many good things were done for small Canadian communities under the Katimavik program. I will have more to say about it in a few minutes.
Mr. Speaker, the budget of the Minister of State (Youth) (Mrs. Champagne) was eliminated, so she is left with a ghost department, the squeleton of a department without a budget and without programs. Naturally we are wondering what kind of role this department will play.
Then, Mr. Speaker, less money available for the Canadian Jobs Strategy program, something like $100 million, and this turned out to be one of the points raised in the secret letter sent by the Minister of State (Youth) to one of her Cabinet colleagues.
If I may quote the English version:
The Minister has not actually given us the French translation as yet. It states: "Public expections created by International Youth Year require careful management". Note the words: "careful management". It goes on: "-especially in light of the significant diminution in youth related spending, close to $100 million since the election".

Mr. Speaker, this means the Department, which is itself responsible for youth admits of course that funds for our youth have been reduced. There is also, Mr. Speaker the $6.2 million cut in the program Challenge 86, and that kind of transfer, that kind of musical chair game that was done with the $30 million which have been transferred from that Challenge 86 program to the Canada census program for this year, under the guise of new funds for the young.
Mr. Speaker, as I said, the budgetary measures show what this Government's priorities are, and another important indication of those priorities are the major studies published by the Government. Looking at the notorious Nielsen Report, we see indeed that the situation of the young in Canada is not a part of their analysis structure. It seems, Mr. Speaker, that all the headlines, the goals, the objectives of the studies do not fit within the context of improving services to the young, but within the national context perhaps, let us say in the context of programs and departments so designated and structured. But clearly, what we see is a lack of emphasis on the youth situation, and we find that most of those studies tend to promote budgetary cuts rather than the priorities of the young people.
I would like to come back, Mr. Speaker, to the importance of employment among the young people. I would like to share a few personal experiences I had when I was 19. I was unemployed for four months. I can very well recall the emotional difficulties, the problems faced by young people when they have no jobs, when they see they have deserving assets

March 12, 1986
Supply
and abilities to contribute to Canadian society. I would like to say that with a Government that is promoting private enterprise, when one has a job, private enterprise is a paradise. This is the best possible example of private enterprise because with jobs young people can look after their own future, their own budget, their own career. But clearly this is impossible when they have no jobs, because they are then dependent upon other people.
If we compare the situation now with what it was 20 years ago, it is clear that for people of my generation, there were a great many more job opportunities which no longer exist. And I feel I was privileged to have access to these job opportunities which do not exist now in such large numbers as they did in the past.
Mr. Speaker, the unemployment rate which was at some 18 per cent among young Canadians rose again last month, which 1 feel is an indication that the Government relies on the private sector to create jobs for young people. As to the programs which will continue to exist, we will see that the situation of young Canadians has a lower priority than before. We have seen that the affirmative action in the Challenge 85 and Challenge 86 programs has been reduced; within the framework of the programs, there are no guarantees for young women; there is no assurance of a fair sharing of jobs before young men and young women; that the wages paid to young women is fair compared to those paid to their male counterparts; that is where this program fails miserably.
Let us go back to Katimavik, Mr. Speaker. As I have already said, this Program has provided many opportunities and had good results in our small communities. Indeed, in my own city of Sioux Lookout, we saw people from Quebec, for instance, who did not speak English before, come to a mostly anglophone community and learn to speak English after four months. I even saw, in native communities, unilingual French or English-speaking people learn a bit of the Native language, Cree, in addition to the other official language. The result has been to create a group of young people who have a better knowledge of Canada, of our transcontinental community than their contemporaries who have had the same opportunity. It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that Katimavik was successful if only because those who took part in this program studied for four years and 60 per cent of what we could call the Katimavik graduates found jobs, 27 per cent in a school or university, and less than 7 per cent of them were unemployed at a time when the unemployment rate among young people generally reached 18 and even 23 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments on the situation in education. There is now an educational anemia in our universities because some people who go to university cannot find a job and take courses without any purpose and without knowing why they attend university.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I will examine the situation of young
native people in this country, young native people who, as my
colleague from Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) said, find themselves in a sad and disastrous situation with respect to employment, with respect to educational opportunities, and with respect to their future as native people in a modern society that hardly appreciate their plight and, in too many cases unfortunately, is not quite prepared to accept them. Mr. Speaker, these young native people are the ones who stand indicted in the Nielsen report where, on page 13 of the English version, one can read the very misleading statement that 70 per cent of those young native people will land in jail before the age of 25. I cannot explain it, it is not up to me to explain it, Mr. Speaker, but I think this refers only to those who are put in institutions, who are re-incarcerated. Such figures are really demoralizing. This being a Government report, I can hardly believe that they are accurate.
So, Mr. Speaker, the whole series of Government measures include precious few programs which promote cultural cooperation between young people and the elderly, programs which in either the native or the majority culture would draw inspiration from the knowledge, the experience and the strong points of elderly Canadians so as to meet the needs of young people in our society who might indeed benefit from the experience of their parents and grandparents.
Mr. Speaker, I see that I have very little time left. I wanted to make a few remarks concerning our Party's task force on youth. I would urge all Hon. Members of the House to read and study the report. The ideas contained in the report are not necessarily our own, for most of them came from various people from coast to coast who are interested in youth programs. Should Hon. Members have any questions, I would be delighted to give further explanations.

Mr. Speaker, the people of Canada are aware that the Minister has a budget of one million dollars up to April 1. This is a million-dollar budget for a non-existent program, for running a department that has no mandate from the Govern-

ment and really only a spokesperson for the Conservative Party. Mr. Speaker, do you know how the young people of Canada refer to the Minister now?

Do you know what the new nickname of the Minister is, Mr. Speaker, the Minister who did not even see fit to stay in this House for this extremely important debate? They call her "bubbles". The reason they call her bubbles is because she sparkles-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, they call her bubbles because she shimmers, she sparkles, she cuts balloons. She spent $24 million during the International Youth Year running around the country. Yet, she is hollow. She has no interior. She has no guts, no heart.
We heard speakers from the Conservative Party today speak time and time again about the private sector. That is the new credo of the Government. What those Hon. Members do not understand-

When the Minister was appointed, she said she was here to speak up for the more fortunate among the young people of Canada. What she fails to understand is .. . for instance in my riding, there are a lot of young unemployed workers who do not have the resources to get into the private sector and start their own business, who don't even know how to read or write, who don't know how to live and behave in the community. Mr. Speaker, the Conservative creed says: the private sector saves, the private sector will take care of everything, but this means ignoring the problems of the young people in our communities who feel lost in our society. It is true they were lost under the
Supply
Liberal Government when we were in a world recession, but now they are looking for a glimmer of hope.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to read a letter about Katimavik, because that was one of the useful programs. There were
20,000	people who became involved in Katimavik, some of whom didn't know for instance what they were going to do after they finished school. We should realize that not everybody in Canada goes to university. And we are here to fight for those people who don't have the financial or mental resources to go to post-secondary institutions and university. We are here to fight for all the young people of Katimavik.
On behalf of the Senator who was laughed at by the Conservatives because they fail to understand the problems of the poor of Canada, I would like to conclude by reading a letter I received from a Katimavik participant.

I think the letter is clear and I would urge Hon. Conservative Members of Parliament who believe in help for the young people of Canada to listen to this very brief letter, and I quote:
1 was very disappointed to hear that Katimavik was being cancelled.
My daughter who is living in England with her sailor husband was in Katimavik some five years ago. She graduated from Grade 13 but wasn't sure what she wanted to do. She heard about Katimavik and decided to go. I can only say that she learned more in nine months about her fellowman, country and many crafts. She was in British Columbia, Rainy River and Quebec.
I'm sure that living with 12 other young people and getting $1 a day and meeting a cross-section of Canadians has certainly made her a better person.
That is the message of Katimavik. That is the message of this motion. I would urge Government Members to listen to Senator Hebert and to reinstate that program and bring some hope to the young people of this country instead of the kind of private sector nonsense we have heard from the Minister, "bubbles" Champagne.
